name: Object Oriented Programming - Design Patterns
scope: A person with BASIC proficiency level in Object Oriented Programming - Design Patterns as a competency should be able to / is capable of explaining and applying OO fundamentals—abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism—plus association, aggregation, composition and dependency in code. They reason with SOLID (especially SRP, OCP), DRY, KISS, YAGNI and basic cohesion/coupling trade-offs. They know the GoF taxonomy (Creational, Structural, Behavioral) and can describe pattern intent, structure and typical use cases. They implement entry-level Creational patterns: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory and surface-level Builder. They implement key Structural patterns: Adapter, Facade, Decorator, and Behavioral patterns: Strategy, Observer, Template Method. They can name remaining GoF patterns and spot anti-patterns such as God Object, Spaghetti Code and Lava Flow. They shortlist patterns for small features, recognise smells like duplicated logic, long conditionals, excessive subclassing, and map them to pattern-based refactors. They write compilable, unit-tested Java/C#/C++/Python/Kotlin/Swift code with proper naming, visibility and packaging. They use modern IDEs (IntelliJ, Eclipse, VS Code, Rider, Xcode), UML/Class/Sequence diagrams, and automated refactorings (rename, extract class/interface, move method). They create unit tests with JUnit/NUnit/pytest, mocks/stubs via Mockito or similar, and maintain Git branches with Maven/Gradle/MSBuild/Make CI pipelines checked by SonarQube, ReSharper, PMD or pylint. They deliver modules or micro-features whose internal design employs patterns, accompanied by concise diagrams and comments, and actively review peer code for pattern alignment. They do not yet architect multi-module systems, craft custom patterns, or tackle nuanced concerns like multithreaded singletons or distributed pattern combinations.
long_scope:
Competency: Object-Oriented Programming – Design Patterns  
Proficiency Band: BASIC (≈ 1–2 years focused, able to operate independently on well-scoped tasks, still guided on architecture-level choices)

————————————————————————————————————————
A. Cognitive & Conceptual Scope
————————————————————————————————————————
1. Core OO Foundations  
   • Precise understanding of abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and how they influence design‐pattern structure and intent.  
   • Recognition of class vs. object relationships (association, aggregation, composition, dependency).

2. Foundational Design Principles  
   • Introductory command of SOLID (knows the five principles, can apply SRP and OCP with coaching).  
   • Grasp of DRY, KISS, YAGNI as rationales for choosing or rejecting a pattern.  
   • Awareness of cohesion / coupling metrics and why patterns manipulate them.

3. Design-Pattern Taxonomy & Intent  
   • Clear mental model of the GoF three families (Creational, Structural, Behavioral).  
   • Thorough knowledge of the “entry-level set” (intent, structure, typical use, trade-offs)  
     ‑ Creational: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory (surface-level), Builder (surface-level)  
     ‑ Structural: Adapter, Facade, Decorator  
     ‑ Behavioral: Strategy, Observer, Template Method  
   • Introductory familiarity with the remaining GoF patterns (can name and loosely categorize each).  
   • First exposure to common anti-patterns that arise when patterns are misapplied (e.g., God Object, Spaghetti Code, Lava Flow).

————————————————————————————————————————
B. Analytical & Problem-Solving Capabilities
————————————————————————————————————————
4. Pattern Selection & Fit Assessment  
   • Given a small feature description, can shortlist and justify 1–2 suitable patterns based on variability points, object lifetime, or communication style.  
   • Can articulate why a pattern is unnecessary when simpler composition or delegation suffices.

5. Code-Smell Recognition (Entry Level)  
   • Detects obvious violations: duplicated logic, long conditional chains, excessive subclassing.  
   • Can map a simple smell to an appropriate “pattern-driven” refactor (e.g., replace conditional with Strategy).

————————————————————————————————————————
C. Implementation & Execution Skills
————————————————————————————————————————
6. Hands-on Coding Competence  
   • Implements the entry-level set of patterns in a mainstream OO language (Java, C#, C++, Python, Kotlin, Swift, etc.) producing compilable, unit-tested code.  
   • Adheres to prescribed naming conventions, visibility rules, and packaging / namespace organization.  
   • Refactors legacy snippets to introduce a pattern without altering observable behavior.

7. Refactoring & Incremental Improvement  
   • Uses IDE automated refactors (rename, extract class, extract interface, move method) to transition to pattern structure.  
   • Maintains backward compatibility via deprecation, adapters or facades when refactoring.

8. Unit-level Validation  
   • Writes automated tests for pattern collaborators (mocks/stubs for Strategy families, observer notifications, decorator chains).  
   • Uses assertions, test coverage and basic mocking frameworks to verify behavioral contracts.

————————————————————————————————————————
D. Documentation, Visualization & Communication
————————————————————————————————————————
9. UML & Lightweight Diagrams  
   • Produces accurate Class and Sequence diagrams for the entry-level set of patterns, reflecting participants, cardinalities and key interactions.  
   • Maintains inline code comments explaining pattern roles and responsibilities without regurgitating textbook prose.

10. Knowledge Transfer  
    • Explains pattern intent and trade-offs to team peers in everyday language.  
    • Participates in code review, identifies missing pattern roles, or redundant hierarchy.

————————————————————————————————————————
E. Tooling & Operational Environment
————————————————————————————————————————
11. Development Toolchain  
    • Daily use of a modern IDE (IntelliJ, Eclipse, VS Code, Rider, Xcode) leveraging:  
      ‑ Built-in UML or plugin pop-ups,  
      ‑ Automated code generation templates for common patterns,  
      ‑ Shortcuts for design-pattern live templates / snippets.  
    • Version control (Git) with branch & merge hygiene suitable for incremental pattern refactoring.

12. Build, Test, Quality Gate  
    • Familiarity with build systems (Maven/Gradle, MSBuild, Make, etc.) and execution of unit-test suites in CI.  
    • Executes static analyzers / linters that flag design smells (SonarQube, ReSharper, PMD, pylint, etc.).

————————————————————————————————————————
F. Expected Outcomes & Deliverables
————————————————————————————————————————
13. Code Artifacts  
    • Modules or micro-features whose internal design employs appropriate patterns, resulting in:  
      ‑ Readable, intention-revealing code,  
      ‑ Reduced duplication,  
      ‑ Clear extension points for new variants.

14. Team Impact  
    • Consistently contributes pattern-aligned code to shared repositories without introducing conflicting paradigms.  
    • Adds concise documentation and diagrams that speed up onboarding of new teammates.

————————————————————————————————————————
G. Boundary of BASIC vs. Adjacent Levels
————————————————————————————————————————
15. Distinguishing Lines  
    • Does not yet architect multi-module systems or create custom patterns; relies on established GoF patterns and mentor guidance.  
    • May overlook nuanced trade-offs (e.g., multithreaded Singleton, performance overhead of Decorator chains) that INTERMEDIATE engineers handle confidently.  
    • Strategy for concurrency, distributed systems, or pattern combinations (e.g., Abstract Factory + Prototype) remains outside current scope.

This comprehensive scope defines the knowledge, skills, tools and outcomes expected from an engineer operating at BASIC proficiency in Object-Oriented Design Patterns, ensuring interview questions can probe breadth of foundational understanding, ability to apply common patterns, and discipline in using standard tooling and documentation practices.
